words.example: He gave a sanctimonious lecture on honesty, though he often cut corners himself.

words.def: Clear, logical and convincing.
words.example: She made a cogent argument for investing in public transport.

words.def: Talking a lot.
words.example: Our loquacious neighbour can turn a quick hello into an hour-long chat.

words.def: Saying very little, and often seeming unfriendly.
words.example: Taciturn by nature, he rarely spoke at family dinners.

words.def: Having or showing great knowledge gained from careful study.
words.example: An erudite historian, she knew the smallest details of medieval trade.

words.def: Full of energy, enthusiasm and good spirits.
words.example: The ebullient crowd cheered as the team walked onto the pitch.

words.def: A calm state of mind, especially in a difficult situation.
words.example: She accepted the bad news with remarkable equanimity.

words.def: A feeling of tiredness and boredom because nothing seems interesting.
words.example: A long, grey winter filled him with a deep sense of ennui.

words.def: Knowing or seeming to know what will happen in the future.
words.example: His prescient article, written years before the crash, described exactly what would go wrong.

words.def: Having a smooth, sweet and pleasant sound.
words.example: The radio host had a mellifluous voice that listeners found calming.

words.def: Not telling the truth; dishonest.
words.example: The mendacious report hid the true cost of the project.

words.def: Strong, clear and effective in expression.
words.example: Critics praised the trenchant analysis of the economic crisis.

words.def: Lacking confidence in yourself and shy about speaking.
words.example: A diffident student, he rarely raised his hand in class.

words.def: Calm self-confidence in a difficult or embarrassing situation.
words.example: She handled the sudden question with great aplomb.

words.def: Changing mood or behaviour suddenly and without a clear reason.
words.example: The capricious weather ruined our plans for the picnic twice.

words.def: Not inclined to talk openly about what you think or feel.
words.example: He was reticent about his past and rarely mentioned his family.

words.def: Expressed briefly and clearly, without unnecessary words.
words.example: A succinct summary of the report fitted on a single slide.

words.def: Something that is very easy to do.
words.example: Don't worry about the interview; for you it will be a piece of cake.

words.def: To relax and not work too hard or worry.
words.example: The doctor told him to take it easy for a few days.

words.def: Time seems to pass very quickly.
words.example: Time flies when you are having fun.

words.def: A cheerful way to tell someone to wake up and get out of bed.
words.example: "Rise and shine! Breakfast is ready," Mum called.

words.def: It is better to do something late than not to do it at all.
words.example: He apologised for the delay, and we agreed that better late than never.

words.def: To say or do something that helps people feel more relaxed when they first meet.
words.example: Handing out coffee on the first morning helped the new students relax and start chatting; it really broke the ice.

words.def: Feeling slightly ill.
words.example: I think I caught a cold, because I have been under the weather since Monday.

words.def: Very rarely.
words.example: My cousin visits us only once in a blue moon, usually at New Year.

words.def: To finish work and stop for now.
words.example: It was nearly midnight, so we decided to call it a day.

words.def: To watch or look after someone or something carefully.
words.example: Please keep an eye on that pasta while I answer the door.

words.def: To start studying hard.
words.example: I can't come out tonight; I need to hit the books before the exam.

words.def: To reveal a secret, by accident or too early.
words.example: She spilled the beans about the wedding before the couple had told anyone.

words.def: A phrase used to give only the main points of a story.
words.example: Long story short, the flight was cancelled and we spent the night at the airport.

words.def: To decide to do something difficult or unpleasant, and get on with it.
words.example: After months of delay, she bit the bullet and sold the old car.

words.text: The ball is in your court
words.def: It is now your turn to take the next step or make a decision.
words.example: We have made our proposal; now the ball is in your court.

words.def: Having the same understanding or opinion about something.
words.example: Before we start, let's make sure we're all on the same page.

words.def: To think in a new and creative way.
words.example: Fitting a garden into such a tiny space forced the designers to be creative, so they had to think outside the box.

words.def: Something that seems bad at first but turns out to be good.
words.example: Missing the flight was a blessing in disguise, because the plane later had technical problems.

words.def: Back at the beginning, having to start again.
words.example: The test failed, so we were back to square one.

words.def: To do something in a cheaper or quicker way, often by ignoring rules or quality.
words.example: The builders cut corners, and the roof started leaking.

words.def: To do more than is expected of you.
words.example: The hotel staff went the extra mile to make our stay special.

words.def: Suddenly and unexpectedly.
words.example: The offer arrived out of the blue, just when she had stopped hoping.

words.def: To get straight to the main point without wasting time.
words.example: Let's cut to the chase: can you finish the work by Friday?

words.def: To avoid saying clearly what you mean, often because it is uncomfortable.
words.example: He kept beating around the bush instead of saying that he wanted to quit.

words.def: To keep working or studying until very late at night.
words.example: She burned the midnight oil to finish the report before the deadline.

words.def: To understand a hidden meaning in what someone says or writes.
words.example: Reading between the lines, I could tell that she was unhappy.

words.text: Take something with a grain of salt
words.def: To not completely believe something.
words.example: He often exaggerates, so I take his stories with a grain of salt.

words.def: A small part of a larger problem that you can see, while the rest stays hidden.
words.example: Those errors were only the tip of the iceberg, and the whole system needed repair.

words.def: To pretend not to notice something that is wrong.
words.example: Some teachers turn a blind eye when students use their phones in class.

words.def: To be very careful about what you say or do so that you do not upset someone.
words.example: After the argument, everyone in the office was walking on eggshells.

words.def: To reach the lowest or worst point.
words.example: After losing his job and his home, he felt he had hit rock bottom.

words.def: To set a higher standard.
words.example: The new phone raises the bar for battery life.

words.def: Having the latest information or knowledge about something.
words.example: It took me two weeks before I was fully up to speed in my new job.

words.def: An obvious, important problem that everyone knows about but avoids discussing.
words.example: Everyone knew the company was losing money, yet it remained the elephant in the room.

words.def: A weakness that can cause someone or something to fail.
words.example: Her lack of patience is her Achilles' heel.

words.def: To argue against an idea, not because you disagree, but to test it.
words.example: I don't believe it myself, but I'll play devil's advocate to test your argument.

words.def: Something that is meant to hide the truth or to distract people.
words.example: The company's promises were all smoke and mirrors.

words.def: A victory won at such a great cost that it is almost a defeat.
words.example: Winning the court case was a Pyrrhic victory, as the legal costs ruined the business.

words.def: To stop something before it can grow into a bigger problem.
words.example: The teacher nipped the bullying in the bud.

words.def: To give your opinion to people who already hold the same view.
words.example: Giving a talk on recycling to an environmental club means preaching to the choir.

words.def: A situation in which you must accept what is offered, because there is no real alternative.
words.example: It was Hobson's choice: take the only flight or miss the wedding.

words.def: Something that distracts you from the real issue or the truth.
words.example: The detective realised that the stolen watch was a red herring.

words.def: A difficult situation in which you cannot escape because the rules work against each other.
words.example: To join the club you need a reference from a member, but nobody will recommend you until you join: a Catch-22.
